newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Copper supply seen ahead of demand to 2000.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Copper supply seen ahead of demand to 2000.

text.p: Copper supply will continue to outpace consumption until at least 2000, brokerage J.B. Were said in a report.
The trend would weigh on copper prices, which are expected to continue to fall in step with a growing surplus, Were said.
Based on market fundamentals, Were said the market could expect to record a supply surplus of 274,000 tonnes this year, growing to 290,000 tonnes in 1998.
In 2000, the surplus should back-track to around 183,000 tonnes, Were said.
However, the key stocks-to-consumption ratio is forecast by Were to reach its highest level in at least six years of 8.4 weeks by then, nearly double the 1996 estimate of 4.3 weeks.
Were left unchanged from its earlier report expectations of an average copper price of US$1.01 a pound in calendar 1996, which is above the current price of about 86 cents a pound.
Subsequent forecasts out to 2000, though, have been revised downward, indicating a more substantial increase in stocks than previously forecast, Were said.
Next year, copper should only fetch 86 cents a pound on average, bottoming out at 76 cents in 1999 before rebounding slightly to 77 cents in 2000, Were said.

Were said recent confirmation that World Bureau of Metals Statsitics (WBMS) had overestimated western world copper consumption in recent years, largely because of double counting, has led it to a 1995 consumption estimate some 137,000 tonnes below its previous figure contained in a report in March.
As a result, the balance of supply and demand has shifted further into surplus through forecasts to 2000, Were said.
A weakened copper price has reduced the potential for financing new copper projects, Were said.
Lower copper prices will also threaten the viability of a number of mines operating at the high end of the industry cost curve, the broker said.
However, many of these mines are protected either by state ownership, subsidies or through hedging programmes for future production, Were said.
"In fact, there are very few high cost mines which we expect to be price sensitive in the short to medium term," Were said.
